title: The Machine That Is Always Falling
blurb: A satellite does not hover. It falls forever, missing the Earth by exactly the right amount, and that is how it stays up.

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Is Always Falling
blocks.text: A satellite is a machine that circles the Earth. It has no motor running all the time. Here is the strange part. A satellite is falling. It moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground, and the missing turns into a circle. Some satellites watch the weather. They see a storm coming before we do. Some send phone calls and shows around the world. Some help a car find the way. The first satellite was called Sputnik. It was the size of a beach ball. All it did was beep.

blocks.prompt: Why Satellites Do Not Fall Down
blocks.text: Throw a ball and it curves down to the grass. Throw it harder and it lands further away. Now imagine throwing it so hard that the Earth curves away underneath it faster than the ball can drop. The ball would never land. It would fall around the whole planet and come back and hit you in the back of the head. That is a satellite. A satellite is not hovering. It is falling, all day, every day. It just moves sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground. The space station is doing it right now, at about seventeen thousand miles an hour. It goes all the way around the Earth in ninety minutes. The astronauts inside watch the sun come up sixteen times a day. Because a satellite never has to push itself along, it barely needs fuel. It spreads out flat wings covered in solar cells, drinks sunlight, and keeps falling for years.

blocks.prompt: The Beeping Ball That Changed Everything
blocks.text: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched a polished metal ball about the size of a beach ball into orbit. It was called Sputnik 1. It weighed roughly as much as a large dog, carried four long antennas, and could do exactly one thing. It beeped. Every 96 minutes it circled the entire planet, sending out a plain radio tone that any person on Earth with a shortwave radio could tune in and hear for themselves. That was the whole mission. No camera, no science instrument, no crew. Just a beep, passing overhead every hour and a half. It terrified people anyway. Americans went outside at dusk to look for the moving spark of light, and understood something quietly enormous: if a machine could be flung over their heads, so could anything else. Within a year the United States founded NASA. Within four years there were humans in orbit. Within twelve there were bootprints on the moon. Sputnik ran out of battery after 21 days and went silent. Three months later it slipped low enough for the air to catch it, and it burned up on the way back down. It had traveled about 43 million miles doing nothing but beeping, and it had started the space age.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Low orbit: about 250 miles up, one lap per 90 minutes
Geostationary: 22,236 miles up, one lap per day
A geostationary satellite looks parked in the sky
GPS satellites orbit about 12,550 miles up
Arthur C. Clarke described the idea in 1945
The higher the orbit, the slower the lap

blocks.prompt: The Satellite That Stands Still
blocks.text: Every satellite is falling. That is not a figure of speech. Gravity pulls on a satellite exactly as it pulls on a dropped apple, and the satellite obeys. The trick is that the satellite is also moving sideways, very fast, and the surface of the Earth curves away beneath it at almost exactly the rate it drops. It falls and falls and never arrives. Isaac Newton worked this out on paper centuries before anyone could build one. He imagined a cannon on a mountaintop so powerful that the ball never came down. Here is where it gets useful. How fast a satellite must travel depends on how high it is. Down low, a couple of hundred miles up, it has to sprint: about 17,000 miles an hour, a full lap in ninety minutes. Climb higher and gravity is weaker, so the required speed drops and the lap takes longer. At 22,236 miles above the equator, the math lands on something remarkable. At that exact altitude a satellite takes 24 hours to complete one orbit. The Earth also takes 24 hours to spin once. The two match. To anyone standing on the ground, that satellite does not move at all. It hangs in the sky like a nail in a wall, day and night, forever. That is why a satellite dish on a house can be bolted in place and never adjusted again. It is aimed at a spot that never moves. A science fiction writer named Arthur C. Clarke described this orbit in a magazine article in 1945, twelve years before Sputnik existed. He worked out that three satellites in that ring could relay signals to nearly the whole planet. He never patented it. He assumed nobody would build such a thing in his lifetime, and he was wrong by decades.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: GPS satellites orbit about 12,550 miles up
Each carries an atomic clock
A receiver needs four satellites, not three
Orbiting clocks run fast by about 38 millionths of a second a day
Uncorrected, GPS would drift about 6 miles a day
Over 30,000 pieces of space junk are tracked

blocks.prompt: The Clocks That Have to Lie About Time
blocks.text: The phone in your pocket knows where it is on the planet to within a few feet, and it does this by listening to clocks that are falling around the Earth. Roughly thirty GPS satellites circle about 12,550 miles overhead, each completing a lap in just under twelve hours. None of them knows you exist. They do not track you, and they never receive anything from you. Each one simply broadcasts, over and over, a plain message that says who it is and precisely what time it is right now. Your phone does all the work. It catches a message, notes that the time stamp inside it is slightly older than the current moment, and multiplies that tiny delay by the speed of light to learn how far away that satellite was. One satellite narrows your position to the surface of an enormous sphere. Two narrow it to a circle. Three narrow it to a point. So why does a receiver need a fourth? Because your phone does not contain an atomic clock. The satellites do, but a phone's cheap clock drifts constantly, and at the speed of light an error of a single millionth of a second becomes a position error of about 1,000 feet. The fourth satellite solves that. With four signals, the receiver has enough information to work out its own clock error and correct it. Your phone is not just finding itself in space. It is fixing its own sense of time, continuously, all day. Then the physics gets stranger. Einstein showed that time is not a fixed background. It runs slower for objects moving quickly, and it runs faster where gravity is weaker. A GPS satellite is doing both at once. It is racing along at roughly 8,700 miles per hour, which drags its clock behind ground clocks by about 7 millionths of a second per day. It is also 12,550 miles above the Earth, where gravity's grip has loosened, which pushes its clock ahead by about 45 millionths of a second per day. The two effects do not cancel. The net result is that every GPS clock in orbit ticks about 38 millionths of a second fast each day. That sounds like nothing. Multiply it by the speed of light and it is not nothing. Left uncorrected, the errors would compound and GPS positions would drift by roughly 6 miles per day, and the whole system would be useless by the end of the first week. So the engineers cheated on purpose. Before launch, the atomic clocks on GPS satellites were deliberately set to tick at the wrong rate, slightly slow, so that once they reached orbit and relativity sped them up, they would be running right. A theory that Einstein published in 1915, with no application in mind whatsoever, is quietly holding up navigation for the entire planet. There is a cost to filling the sky. More than 30,000 pieces of debris are tracked in orbit right now: dead satellites, spent rocket stages, fragments of old collisions. At orbital speed, a fleck of paint hits with the force of a bullet. In 1978 a NASA scientist named Donald Kessler warned that if the junk grew dense enough, one collision could scatter fragments that caused more collisions, and the cascade could seal low orbit off for generations. We are still adding satellites, faster now than ever.
